title: A Quadratic Lens on Muon’s Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton–Schulz†

paper.title: A Quadratic Lens on Muon’s Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton–Schulz †
paper.abstract: Abstract Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a strong optimizer for training large neural networks. It has matched or outperformed AdamW in language-model pretraining, from speedrun benchmarks ( Jordan et al., 2024a ) to large-scale training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) , and standard optimizers more broadly in vision ( Jordan et al., 2024b ; Pethick et al., 2025 ) , diffusion ( Schaipp, 2025 ) , and tabular models ( Gorishniy et al., 2026 ) . For two-dimensional parameter blocks, Muon approximately orthogonalizes the momentum matrix with a few Newton--Schulz iterations, that is, it steps along an approximation of the polar factor polar ⁡ ( G ) = U ​ V ⊤ \mathrm{polar}(G)=UV^{\top} of G = U ​ Σ G ​ V ⊤ G=U\Sigma_{G}V^{\top} . The same direction is shared by a broader family of matrix optimizers. It is the steepest-descent direction for the spectral norm, used in stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015a ; Carlson et al., 2016 ; Carlson et al., 2015b ) and revisited by Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) . It is also the linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) direction of norm-constrained methods ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) reduces to it when preconditioner accumulation is switched off ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . Controlled benchmarks place such matrix-based optimizers among the strongest available ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , so understanding when a step along polar ⁡ ( G ) \mathrm{polar}(G) helps matters well beyond Muon . Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) . We study this question on matrix quadratics. Quadratic models are the classical setting for understanding optimizers, and they have repeatedly explained optimizer behavior in deep learning, from critical batch sizes and the value of preconditioning ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) to the advantage of Adam on transformers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and of sign descent under Zipf-distributed data ( Kunstner and Bach, 2025 ) . Their matrix-valued form already contains the features that matter for orthogonalized updates: singular structure, anisotropic curvature, dependence on initialization, and the choice of coordinate system. We focus on the core update of Muon and of the methods above, X k + 1 = X k − γ k ​ polar ​ ( ∇ f ​ ( X k ) ) X_{k+1}=X_{k}-\gamma_{k}\mathrm{polar}(\nabla f(X_{k})) , and compare it with GD and SignGD . We call this update PolarGD by analogy with SignGD : it replaces the gradient by its polar factor, as SignGD replaces it by its entrywise sign (it has also been called spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2016 ) ). Momentum and stochasticity are left out on purpose, so that the effect of the update direction can be isolated. To compare the three directions on equal footing, we let each take its best scalar step, computed by exact line search. This removes learning-rate tuning from the comparison, so that methods are compared through their directions rather than through step-size choices. On matrix quadratics, the resulting one-step decreases are available in closed form and show a tradeoff between how much a direction D D decreases the loss to first order, its gain ⟨ G , D ⟩ \langle G,D\rangle , and the curvature tr ⁡ ( D ⊤ ​ H ​ D ) \mathrm{tr}(D^{\top}HD) along it.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our main contributions are as follows. • One-step geometry (Section 3 ). We give closed-form line-search decreases for GD , SignGD , and PolarGD . Each method reaches the minimizer in one step under its own condition (Theorem 1 ): GD from every starting point only when the Hessian is a multiple of the identity, SignGD when the error has entries of equal magnitude and the Hessian preserves their signs (e.g., a diagonal Hessian), and PolarGD , for any positive-definite Hessian, when the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms. This explains why orthogonal initialization is special for PolarGD and diagonal structure for SignGD . In the worst case over iterates, however, the one-step comparison is pessimistic for PolarGD : its guaranteed decrease is smaller than GD ’s (Theorem 3 ), although PolarGD is often faster over whole trajectories (Figure 1 ). • Rotation equivariance (Section 3.3 ). PolarGD is equivariant under orthogonal changes of basis, while SignGD is not (Theorem 2 ): rotating the problem rotates the PolarGD iterates but changes the SignGD trajectory. Accordingly, PolarGD keeps its performance when an ill-conditioned diagonal problem, such as a Zipf-type regression model of language data, is rotated, whereas SignGD degrades. • Implicit preconditioning (Section 4 ). PolarGD is a gradient step with a preconditioner set by the current iterate, whose condition number is that of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. When the iterate has full row rank, this gives an exact formula for the progress per step, for line search and fixed steps. With line search, GD satisfies f ⁡ ( X k + 1 ) ≤ ( 1 − 1 / κ ⁡ ( H ) ) ​ f ​ ( X k ) f(X_{k+1})\leq(1-1/\kappa(H))\,f(X_{k}) ; PolarGD satisfies the same bound with the condition number κ ⁡ ( H ) \kappa(H) of the Hessian replaced by the condition number κ ⁡ ( X k ) \kappa(X_{k}) of the iterate (taking X ⋆ = 0 X^{\star}=0 ). PolarGD is therefore fastest when the rows of X k X_{k} are orthogonal with equal norms and slowest when X k X_{k} has tiny singular values; this slow regime is tight, and in it GD can be nearly one-step exact while PolarGD stays slow along the trajectory. We also show that a direction that is better for one step need not give a faster trajectory. • Rank deficiency and finite Newton--Schulz (Section 4.2 ). We extend these identities to rank-deficient iterates and show that a few Newton--Schulz steps, as used in Muon , give a softened polar update: they behave like damped polar, treating large singular values like exact polar and tiny ones like a GD step. Near rank deficiency this converges faster than exact polar, so finite Newton--Schulz is not merely an approximation of the polar factor.

sections.heading: Related and concurrent work.
sections.text: Gonon et al. (2026) also study Muon on quadratics. On the isotropic quadratic, exact polar steps with a constant step size can fail to reach the minimizer, and random perturbations of the polar step restore reachability in a one-dimensional model; on general Hessians, they show numerically that the comparison with GD depends on the shape of the spectrum, that Newton--Schulz can help or hurt, and that a direction that wins at every step need not win along the trajectory. Our one-step and trajectory results are exact for any positive-definite Hessian. We relate our one-step condition to Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2025) in Section 2 and discuss other work in the sections where it is relevant.

sections.heading: Zipf Laws experiment.
sections.text: Kunstner and Bach (2025) model next-token prediction as linear regression over one-hot inputs, with squared loss L ⁡ ( X ) = 1 2 ​ n ​ ‖ Z ​ X − Y ‖ F 2 L(X)=\frac{1}{2n}\|ZX-Y\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} . Since one-hot inputs are orthogonal, Z ⊤ ​ Z Z^{\top}Z is diagonal with entries given by token counts; under Zipf frequencies π k ∝ k − ζ \pi_{k}\propto k^{-\zeta} , this gives ( 6 ) with H = diag ⁡ ( π 1 , … , π d ) H=\mathrm{diag}(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{d}) and a target X ⋆ X^{\star} of next-token probabilities. On such ill-conditioned diagonal problems, SignGD scales much more favorably than GD ( Kunstner and Bach, 2025 ) ; heavy-tailed frequencies of this kind slow GD on rare classes but not sign-based methods, which Kunstner et al. (2024) identify as a reason for Adam ’s advantage on language models. Figure 2 shows that PolarGD behaves similarly in the diagonal case (if H H and X − X ⋆ X-X^{\star} are diagonal and d = m d=m , then Q = sign ⁡ ( G ) Q=\mathrm{sign}(G) ; App. B.2 ) and that, unlike SignGD , it keeps its performance when H H is randomly rotated; the advantage of sign descent requires curvature concentrated on the diagonal ( Balles et al., 2020 ) , which a rotation removes. Theorem 2 guarantees this when H H and X ⋆ X^{\star} are rotated together; Figure 2 keeps X ⋆ X^{\star} fixed and confirms it empirically, and App. A.3 shows both cases. This is consistent with, though not by itself an explanation of, the strong performance of Muon in language modeling.

sections.heading: From one step to trajectories.
sections.text: Theorem 1 explains why row-isotropic iterates are special, and Theorem 2 why PolarGD behaves the same on diagonal and rotated Hessians. Neither explains the stronger phenomenon in Figures 1 and 2 : PolarGD stays fast along the whole trajectory when H H is dense and ill-conditioned. Section 4 shows that the polar direction is a gradient step preconditioned by the iterate covariance X ​ X ⊤ XX^{\top} rather than by H H , which explains why row-isotropic iterates can be fast for any κ ⁡ ( H ) \kappa(H) and why near-rank-deficient iterates are slow. On our quadratic loss, PolarGD is empirically as robust to ill-conditioning as SignGD (explained in Section 4 ). Unlike SignGD , it is orthogonally equivariant, so its performance carries over to every rotation of a problem, not only to coordinate-aligned ones.

sections.heading: 4 Beyond One Step: Implicit Preconditioning
sections.text: The polar direction can be rewritten as a gradient step with a preconditioner set by the row covariance X ​ X ⊤ XX^{\top} of the current iterate rather than by H H alone. This yields an optimistic regime, where row-isotropic iterates cancel the curvature, and a pessimistic one, where tiny singular values make the preconditioner ill-conditioned. We first note that one-step preferences can change along a trajectory (see also Appendix C ).

sections.heading: Local preferences need not be consistent along a trajectory.
sections.text: Even on convex quadratics, the sign of Δ Pol ​ ( X ) − Δ GD ​ ( X ) \Delta_{\mathrm{Pol}}(X)-\Delta_{\mathrm{GD}}(X) can change with X X , so pointwise one-step comparisons do not induce a global ordering between methods. Appendix C gives a closed-form 2 × 2 2\times 2 diagonal example in which, along the exact-line-search GD trajectory { X k GD } k ≥ 0 \{X_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}\}_{k\geq 0} , the local winner between GD and PolarGD alternates deterministically at every iterate. Gonon et al. (2026) give a numerical example of a related failure: a greedy rule that picks the better of the two directions chooses the polar direction at every step and is still much slower than GD with line search. Both examples call for the trajectory-level analysis below.

sections.heading: Relation to prior preconditioning views.
sections.text: Writing polar ( G ) = ( G G ⊤ ) − 1 / 2 G \mathrm{polar}(G)=(GG^{\top})^{-1/2}G as a gradient-built preconditioner is common ( Lau et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) ; on quadratics, substituting G = H ​ X G=HX shows that this preconditioner is set by the iterate, with conditioning κ ⁡ ( X ) \kappa(X) whatever H H is (Proposition 2 ). Under smoothness and the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, Lau et al. (2025) prove linear rates for the dual-adapted step that depend on κ ⁡ ( H ) \kappa(H) , such as 1 − 1 / ( r ​ κ ​ ( H ) ) 1-1/(r\kappa(H)) for gradients of rank r r ; on quadratics, the first lower bound in ( 16 ) has this form and is tight, so this dependence cannot be removed in the worst case, while the second bound depends on κ ⁡ ( X ) \kappa(X) alone. When H H and X ​ X ⊤ XX^{\top} commute, Q = polar ⁡ ( X ) Q=\mathrm{polar}(X) and H H drops out of the direction (Corollary 4 ). Ma et al. (2026) exploit decoupling of this kind, along trajectories aligned with the eigenbasis of the problem and with geometrically decaying steps, to prove rates independent of the condition number for matrix factorization and for an in-context-learning quadratic, and leave matrix linear regression, the setting studied here, open.

sections.heading: Greedy steps are not the best fixed steps.
sections.text: For GD , exact line search typically does at least as well as a tuned fixed step; for PolarGD and SignGD it does not (Figure 10 ; Appendix D gives further settings). In the dual-adapted parameterization, line search is the fixed rate α = 1 \alpha=1 in ( 17 ), which maximizes the one-step factor, yet the tuned rate α ≈ 1.7 \alpha\approx 1.7 converges much faster: it keeps p ⁡ ( X k ) p(X_{k}) near 0.6 0.6 , whereas under line search p ⁡ ( X k ) p(X_{k}) decays to 0.01 0.01 within 150 150 iterations. Line search itself creates the tiny singular values that make p ⁡ ( X ) p(X) small. When H H and X ​ X ⊤ XX^{\top} commute, a fixed step maps the singular values of X X to s i + = | s i − α ​ s ¯ H | s_{i}^{+}=|s_{i}-\alpha\bar{s}_{H}| , where s ¯ H \bar{s}_{H} is their λ \lambda -weighted mean (Corollary 4 ). Line search subtracts the mean, which lies in the bulk of the spectrum, so singular values near it are sent close to zero and a growing tail of tiny ones forms; a longer step instead reflects small singular values to large ones. As in Figure 3 , the locally optimal choice is not optimal along the trajectory, and the gap grows with κ ⁡ ( H ) \kappa(H) (Figure 10 (c)). On our quadratic loss, PolarGD acts like a self-preconditioned GD step: the polar map sets all singular values of the gradient to one, so the effective preconditioner is controlled by the iterate covariance X ​ X ⊤ XX^{\top} , not by κ ⁡ ( H ) \kappa(H) alone. This helps near row-isotropic iterates, but can be pessimistic near rank deficiency, where exact polar normalization gives tiny singular modes the same weight as large ones.

Thus rank deficiency is an active-subspace regime rather than a failure of the theory. Appendix E.6 gives the full projector-based extension.

sections.heading: 4.2 Near-Rank-Deficiency and Softened Polar Updates
sections.text: The representation Q = ( G G ⊤ ) † / 2 G Q=(GG^{\top})^{\dagger/2}G also exposes a failure mode of exact polar normalization: tiny nonzero singular values are inverted. Two simple variants reduce this sensitivity: rank-truncated polar, Q ( s ) := U : , 1 : s V : , 1 : s ⊤ Q^{(s)}:=U_{:,1:s}V_{:,1:s}^{\top} , which drops small modes, and damped polar, Q ε := ( G G ⊤ + ε I d ) − 1 / 2 G , Q_{\varepsilon}:=(GG^{\top}+\varepsilon I_{d})^{-1/2}G, which maps each singular value to σ i / σ i 2 + ε \sigma_{i}/\sqrt{\sigma_{i}^{2}+\varepsilon} . Up to the factor ε \sqrt{\varepsilon} , damped polar is the soft spectral clipping ( I d + G G ⊤ / c 2 ) − 1 / 2 G (I_{d}+GG^{\top}/c^{2})^{-1/2}G with c = ε c=\sqrt{\varepsilon} , a smooth version of σ i ↦ min ⁡ ( σ i , c ) \sigma_{i}\mapsto\min(\sigma_{i},c) , which Jiang et al. (2026) apply to the updates of AdamW -type optimizers; there c c is large and only the largest singular values are capped, whereas Muon operates in the opposite regime. We define these variants and give basic properties in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Finite Newton--Schulz as damped polar.
sections.text: Practical Muon replaces the SVD by q q Newton--Schulz steps on G / ‖ G ‖ F G/\left\lVert G\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}} , which keep the singular vectors of G G and map each normalized singular value s s to ϕ q ​ ( s ) \phi_{q}(s) (Appendix G ). Small singular values are multiplied by a fixed factor ℓ q \ell_{q} , which grows geometrically with q q ( ℓ 5 ≈ 485 \ell_{5}\approx 485 for Muon ’s coefficients), while those above about 1 / ℓ q 1/\ell_{q} are mapped close to 1 1 . This is the behavior of damped polar with ε q = ℓ q − 2 \varepsilon_{q}=\ell_{q}^{-2} , i.e., a rescaled soft spectral clipping at c = 1 / ℓ q c=1/\ell_{q} : finite Newton--Schulz acts like GD on singular values below the damping scale 1 / ℓ q 1/\ell_{q} and like exact polar above it, and its damping decreases geometrically with the number of steps. Near rank deficiency it therefore avoids the slow regime of exact polar, and fewer steps converge faster (Figure 4 ). This contrasts with convergence bounds that treat the Newton--Schulz error only as a degradation factor ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ) : here a less accurate polar factor converges faster. Gonon et al. (2026) observe numerically that five Newton--Schulz steps can beat exact polar on some quadratics; damping of tiny singular values gives a deterministic mechanism for such gains. sections.heading: Newton--Schulz in practice.
sections.text: To check whether this regime occurs in practice, we examined a 90M-parameter transformer trained with Muon on 1.8B tokens (App. H ). Figure 5 (a) shows the singular values of the momentum matrices M M that Muon orthogonalizes, normalized by ‖ M ‖ F \left\lVert M\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}} as in training. About a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices lie below the damping scale 1 / ℓ 5 ≈ 2 ⋅ 10 − 3 1/\ell_{5}\approx 2\cdot 10^{-3} , where five Newton--Schulz steps act like GD rather than like exact polar; the MLP matrices, the embedding, and the LM head have none. Over all 50 matrices, exact polar would place about 16% of the update’s squared Frobenius norm on these directions and five Newton--Schulz steps about 5%. The effect is strongly heterogeneous (Figure 5 (b)): it is largest in the first layer and decreases with depth. As in NanoGPT ( Shulgin et al., 2026 , Figure 5) , attention matrices are thus much harder to orthogonalize than MLP matrices, and their smallest singular values explain why: Newton--Schulz becomes polar-like on all directions only once ℓ q \ell_{q} times the smallest normalized singular value exceeds 1 1 , which takes 9–18 steps for the attention matrices and 4–5 for the MLP matrices.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We isolated the geometry of the orthogonalized update shared by Muon and related matrix optimizers by analyzing PolarGD on matrix quadratics. PolarGD benefits from orthogonal equivariance and implicit preconditioning by the iterate, but it is not uniformly better than GD or SignGD : it is fast near row-isotropic iterates and slow near rank deficiency, where exact polar normalization overweights tiny singular values. Finite Newton--Schulz softens the update exactly there and can then converge faster than exact polar, so it is not merely an approximation of the polar factor. The trajectory results rely on the quadratic structure, but Proposition 1 only needs the curvature bounds ( 2 ), and equivariance and the softening by Newton--Schulz hold for any objective, including the momentum matrix that Muon orthogonalizes. Our transformer measurements show that the regime where exact polar and Newton--Schulz differ occurs in practice. This suggests treating the number of Newton--Schulz steps, or the damping level, as a design choice of the optimizer rather than only as an accuracy setting.

sections.heading: A.1 Learning Rate Selection
sections.text: Unless stated otherwise, whenever we report results for a “best-tuned” learning rate, the following two-stage grid search is applied. In the first stage, we evaluate 50 50 learning rates drawn from an evenly-spaced logarithmic grid over [ 10 − 8 , 10 2 ] [10^{-8},10^{2}] . We select the candidate γ c \gamma_{c} that minimizes the loss at the final iterate among runs that did not diverge. In the second stage, we evaluate a further 50 points on a finer logarithmic interval [ γ c 10 , 10 ​ γ c ] [\frac{\gamma_{c}}{10},10\gamma_{c}] . The final reported learning rate is the one whose run first crosses a threshold of ε \varepsilon (in the least number of iterates). If no run reaches this threshold, we select the run which minimizes the loss at the final iterate. sections.heading: Hessian Structures.
sections.text: We test three specific curvature profiles to isolate the effects of condition number and coordinate alignment. To model Hessians arising in ill-conditioned, multi-output regression problems, we draw random matrices from the Marchenko–Pastur (MP) ensemble: H = 1 N ​ Z 𝖳 ​ Z , Z ∈ ℝ N × d , Z i ​ j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) H=\frac{1}{N}Z^{\mathsf{T}}Z,\qquad Z\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d},\quad Z_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) Here the aspect ratio d / N ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] d/N\in(0,1] (the ratio of input features to samples) dictates the conditioning. Using this framework, we construct the following Hessian regimes • Isotropic Hessian: H = I d H=I_{d} . This regime has condition number κ = 1 \kappa=1 . • Dense: H = 1 N ​ Z 𝖳 ​ Z H=\frac{1}{N}Z^{\mathsf{T}}Z with d / N = 0.8 d/N=0.8 . • Diagonal: H = diag ⁡ ( λ 1 , … , λ d ) H=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}) , where λ i \lambda_{i} are the exact eigenvalues of the dense MP matrix.

sections.heading: A.3 Zipfian Language-Modeling Proxy (Figure 2 )
sections.text: To evaluate how these optimizers perform under the heavy-tailed geometries typical of language modeling, we construct a multi-output linear regression proxy inspired by Kunstner and Bach (2025) .

sections.heading: Linear Bigram Model.
sections.text: Consider fitting a linear next-token prediction model X ∈ ℝ d × d X\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} on n n token pairs z i , y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } d z_{i},y_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{d} representing one-hot encodings. The squared loss is given by L ⁡ ( X ) = 1 2 ​ n ​ ‖ Z ​ X − Y ‖ F 2 , L(X)=\frac{1}{2n}\|ZX-Y\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}, where X i ​ j X_{ij} is an estimate of p ⁡ ( token j ∣ token i ) p(\text{token}_{j}\mid\text{token}_{i}) for each i , j ∈ [ d ] i,j\in[d] . To simulate the heavy-tailed nature of language modeling, token frequencies follow a Zipfian distribution π k ∝ k − ζ \pi_{k}\propto k^{-\zeta} where ζ > 0 \zeta>0 controls the heaviness of the tail. Following their framework, we consider the equivalent quadratic problem f ⁡ ( X ) = 1 2 ​ tr ​ ( ( X − X ⋆ ) 𝖳 ​ H ​ ( X − X ⋆ ) ) , f(X)=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}((X-X^{\star})^{\mathsf{T}}H(X-X^{\star})), initialized at X 0 = 0 X_{0}=0 , with Hessian H = diag ⁡ ( π 1 , … , π d ) H=\mathrm{diag}(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{d}) and target X i ​ j ⋆ = p ⁡ ( token j ∣ token i ) X^{\star}_{ij}=p(\text{token}_{j}\mid\text{token}_{i}) . We draw each row of X ⋆ X^{\star} independently from a Dirichlet distribution with parameter 100 ​ π 100\,\pi , so that the next-token distributions fluctuate around the Zipf frequencies; X ⋆ X^{\star} then has full rank almost surely. A full-rank target matters: for a rank-one target such as 𝟏 ​ π 𝖳 \mathbf{1}\pi^{\mathsf{T}} (every row equal to π \pi ), every gradient H ⁡ ( X k − X ⋆ ) H(X_{k}-X^{\star}) from X 0 = 0 X_{0}=0 is rank one, so dual-adapted PolarGD coincides with GD .

sections.text: To test the rotation dependence of the optimizers, we additionally evaluate a rotated setting: H = R 𝖳 ​ diag ​ ( π ) ​ R H=R^{\mathsf{T}}\mathrm{diag}(\pi)R , where R ∈ ℝ d × d R\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a random orthogonal matrix. This rotation preserves the spectrum while removing axis alignment. This approach follows recent work by Zhang et al. (2025) , which demonstrates that Adam is highly sensitive to random rotations. We rotate the Hessian in two ways (Figure 6 ). (i) As in Figure 2 , the target X ⋆ X^{\star} is kept fixed in the standard basis. For GD and PolarGD , this is equivalent to keeping H H diagonal and replacing the target by R ​ X ⋆ RX^{\star} , so it changes the problem and is not covered by Theorem 2 . sections.heading: Experimental implication.
sections.text: Because of Proposition 3 , “rotating” a diagonal Hessian by an orthogonal change of basis should not change GD or PolarGD behavior (up to the corresponding rotation of the initialization), while it can substantially change SignGD behavior. This separation helps design experiments that isolate truly spectral effects ( PolarGD ) from coordinate effects ( SignGD ).

sections.heading: D.2 Line Search on a CIFAR-5K MLP
sections.text: We evaluate on a two-layer fully-connected network with ReLU activations, following the CIFAR-5K testbed of Cohen et al. (2021) , a subsampled collection of the CIFAR-10 dataset ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) consisting of 5 5 classes, each with 1,000 1,000 samples. The architecture has input dimension d in = 3,072 d_{\mathrm{in}}=3{,}072 (flattened 32 × 32 × 3 32\times 32\times 3 images), hidden dimension h = 4,608 h=4{,}608 ( = 1.5 ​ d in =1.5\,d_{\mathrm{in}} ), output dimension 5 5 , and no bias terms; weights are initialized via Kaiming normal initialization ( He et al., 2015 ) . We train with cross-entropy loss. We compare standard gradient descent ( GD ) and PolarGD (the core Muon update without momentum); PolarGD applies the polar direction to both weight matrices. Since we are in the full batch setting with no momentum, the only hyperparameter is the step size. For each optimizer we evaluate (i) a grid of fixed learning rates and (ii) an exact line search implemented via Brent’s method, which searches for the step size in the wide interval [ 0 , 4 ] [0,4] with tolerance 10 − 5 10^{-5} ; each line-search step requires approximately 10 10 – 15 15 forward passes. All runs share a fixed random seed and are trained for 100 100 iterations. Figure 11 : Line search on an MLP. Training loss on CIFAR-5K under fixed dual-adapted learning rates and line search (dashed). The three fixed rates shown are the best-performing from a grid search. For GD , line search matches or slightly beats the best fixed rate; for PolarGD , a fixed learning rate outperforms it. This is consistent with the local-global gap observed in the quadratic case (Section 4 ). The rightmost panel plots the line-search step size: for GD it oscillates, whereas for PolarGD it decays by about an order of magnitude over 100 iterations.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: For every ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , the iterate is full rank, so full-row-rank PolarGD pays curvature tr ⁡ ( H ) = μ + ( d − 1 ) ​ L \mathrm{tr}(H)=\mu+(d-1)L . However, as ε ↓ 0 \varepsilon\downarrow 0 , almost all gradient gain is concentrated in the first, low-curvature direction. Exact polar normalization still maps the tiny singular modes L ​ ε L\varepsilon to unit-size directions, so the line-search denominator pays for all directions even though most of the gain comes from only one. At the limiting point ε = 0 \varepsilon=0 , the gradient is rank one. Then PolarGD and GD are collinear, and the active-subspace formula from Appendix E.6 uses the active curvature tr ⁡ ( H ​ Π G ) = μ \mathrm{tr}(H\Pi_{G})=\mu instead of tr ⁡ ( H ) \mathrm{tr}(H) . In that rank-one limit, PolarGD again reaches the minimizer in one step. Hence the pathology is a near-rank-deficient full-rank effect: exact polar is discontinuous at rank drops because it hard-normalizes every nonzero singular mode. This is the failure mode targeted by rank truncation, damping, and finite Newton--Schulz filters.

sections.heading: Where the GD -like range occurs.
sections.text: All singular values in the GD -like range belong to attention matrices, where they make up about a quarter of all singular values; the MLP matrices, the embedding, and the LM head have none. The fraction is largest in the first layer (89% for the query matrix and 60% for the output projection at the final checkpoint) and decreases with depth (Figure 5 (b)). The momentum spectra are nearly stationary over training (Figure 12 ), whereas the raw gradients have many more singular values in the GD -like range early in training (about 40% for attention at 25–50% of training) and about as many as the momentum at the end: momentum averaging stabilizes the spectrum that Newton--Schulz receives. Other cutoffs than 1 / ℓ 5 1/\ell_{5} change the percentages (between 5 % 5\% and 28 % 28\% for attention at the final checkpoint) but not this pattern. Figure 12 : (Left, middle) Distribution of the normalized singular values of the momentum matrices at four checkpoints, for the attention matrices (left) and for the MLP, embedding, and LM-head matrices (middle); the shaded band is the GD -like range. (Right) Percentage of singular values in the GD -like range over training for the momentum M M and the raw gradient G G , for the attention matrices and for all 50 matrices.

sections.heading: Relation to the weights.
sections.text: In the quadratic model, tiny singular values of the gradient come from tiny singular values of the iterate. Here the attention weights are themselves ill-conditioned, but the GD -like directions of M M are not aligned with the bottom singular directions of the weights: for the span of the k k left (right) singular vectors of M M with s i < 1.1 ⋅ 10 − 3 s_{i}<1.1\cdot 10^{-3} (where ϕ 5 ​ ( s i ) < 1 2 \phi_{5}(s_{i})<\tfrac{1}{2} ) and the span of the k k bottom left (right) singular vectors of the weight matrix, the mean squared cosine of the principal angles is, in the median over the 32 32 matrices with such directions at the final checkpoint, 1.05 1.05 ( 1.02 1.02 ) times its value k / n k/n for a random k k -dimensional subspace of ℝ n \mathbb{R}^{n} . transfer literally.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.30280v1 [cs.LG] 21 Oct 2026 A Quadratic Lens on Muon’s Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton–Schulz † Egor Shulgin Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Saudi Arabia Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), United Arab Emirates Sam Laing Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen and MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center, Germany Affiliation: OpenEuroLLM Antonio Orvieto Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen and MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center, Germany Peter Richtárik Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Saudi Arabia Abstract Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime. $\ast$ $\ast$ footnotetext: Equal contribution. Correspondence to Egor Shulgin, shulgin.yegor@gmail.com . $\dagger$ $\dagger$ footnotetext: A shorter version of this work was presented at the ICML 2026 Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics. $\ddagger$ $\ddagger$ footnotetext: The initial versions of this work were completed while Egor Shulgin was at KAUST. 1 Introduction Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a strong optimizer for training large neural networks. It has matched or outperformed AdamW in language-model pretraining, from speedrun benchmarks ( Jordan et al., 2024a ) to large-scale training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) , and standard optimizers more broadly in vision ( Jordan et al., 2024b ; Pethick et al., 2025 ) , diffusion ( Schaipp, 2025 ) , and tabular models ( Gorishniy et al., 2026 ) . For two-dimensional parameter blocks, Muon approximately orthogonalizes the momentum matrix with a few Newton--Schulz iterations, that is, it steps along an approximation of the polar factor polar ⁡ ( G ) = U ​ V ⊤ \mathrm{polar}(G)=UV^{	op} of G = U ​ Σ G ​ V ⊤ G=U\Sigma_{G}V^{	op} . The same direction is shared by a broader family of matrix optimizers. It is the steepest-descent direction for the spectral norm, used in stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015a ; Carlson et al., 2016 ; Carlson et al., 2015b ) and revisited by Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) . It is also the linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) direction of norm-constrained methods ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) reduces to it when preconditioner accumulation is switched off ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . Controlled benchmarks place such matrix-based optimizers among the strongest available ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , so understanding when a step along polar ⁡ ( G ) \mathrm{polar}(G) helps matters well beyond Muon . Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) . We study this question on matrix quadratics. Quadratic models are the classical setting for understanding optimizers, and they have repeatedly explained optimizer behavior in deep learning, from critical batch sizes and the value of preconditioning ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) to the advantage of Adam on transformers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and of sign descent under Zipf-distributed data ( Kunstner and Bach, 2025 ) . Their matrix-valued form already contains the features that matter for orthogonalized updates: singular structure, anisotropic curvature, dependence on initialization, and the choice of coordinate system. We call this update PolarGD by analogy with SignGD : it replaces the gradient by its polar factor, as SignGD replaces it by its entrywise sign (it has also been called spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2016 ) ). Momentum and stochasticity are left out on purpose, so that the effect of the update direction can be isolated. To compare the three directions on equal footing, we let each take its best scalar step, computed by exact line search. This removes learning-rate tuning from the comparison, so that methods are compared through their directions rather than through step-size choices. On matrix quadratics, the resulting one-step decreases are available in closed form and show a tradeoff between how much a direction D D decreases the loss to first order, its gain ⟨ G , D ⟩ \langle G,Dangle , and the curvature tr ⁡ ( D ⊤ ​ H ​ D ) \mathrm{tr}(D^{	op}HD) along it. Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows. • One-step geometry (Section 3 ). We give closed-form line-search decreases for GD , SignGD , and PolarGD . Each method reaches the minimizer in one step under its own condition (Theorem 1 ): GD from every starting point only when the Hessian is a multiple of the identity, SignGD when the error has entries of equal magnitude and the Hessian preserves their signs (e.g., a diagonal Hessian), and PolarGD , for any positive-definite Hessian, when the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms. This explains why orthogonal initialization is special for PolarGD and diagonal structure for SignGD . In the worst case over iterates, however, the one-step comparison is pessimistic for PolarGD : its guaranteed decrease is smaller than GD ’s (Theorem 3 ), although PolarGD is often faster over whole trajectories (Figure 1 ). • Rotation equivariance (Section 3.3 ). PolarGD is equivariant under orthogonal changes of basis, while SignGD is not (Theorem 2 ): rotating the problem rotates the PolarGD iterates but changes the SignGD trajectory. Accordingly, PolarGD keeps its performance when an ill-conditioned diagonal problem, such as a Zipf-type regression model of language data, is rotated, whereas SignGD degrades. • Implicit preconditioning (Section 4 ). PolarGD is a gradient step with a preconditioner set by the current iterate, whose condition number is that of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. When the iterate has full row rank, this gives an exact formula for the progress per step, for line search and fixed steps. With line search, GD satisfies f ⁡ ( X k + 1 ) ≤ ( 1 − 1 / κ ⁡ ( H ) ) ​ f ​ ( X k ) f(X_{k+1})\leq(1-1/\kappa(H))\,f(X_{k}) ; PolarGD satisfies the same bound with the condition number κ ⁡ ( H ) \kappa(H) of the Hessian replaced by the condition number κ ⁡ ( X k ) \kappa(X_{k}) of the iterate (taking X ⋆ = 0 X^{\star}=0 ). PolarGD is therefore fastest when the rows of X k X_{k} are orthogonal with equal norms and slowest when X k X_{k} has tiny singular values; this slow regime is tight, and in it GD can be nearly one-step exact while PolarGD stays slow along the trajectory. We also show that a direction that is better for one step need not give a faster trajectory. • Rank deficiency and finite Newton--Schulz (Section 4.2 ). We extend these identities to rank-deficient iterates and show that a few Newton--Schulz steps, as used in Muon , give a softened polar update: they behave like damped polar, treating large singular values like exact polar and tiny ones like a GD step. Near rank deficiency this converges faster than exact polar, so finite Newton--Schulz is not merely an approximation of the polar factor. Related and concurrent work. Gonon et al. (2026) also study Muon on quadratics. On the isotropic quadratic, exact polar steps with a constant step size can fail to reach the minimizer, and random perturbations of the polar step restore reachability in a one-dimensional model; on general Hessians, they show numerically that the comparison with GD depends on the shape of the spectrum, that Newton--Schulz can help or hurt, and that a direction that wins at every step need not win along the trajectory. Our one-step and trajectory results are exact for any positive-definite Hessian.
